newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. Council renews Haiti force for final 4 months.
newsitem.headline: U.N. Council renews Haiti force for final 4 months.

text.p: The Security Council on Wednesday voted to extend the United Nations military and police force in troubled Haiti for a final four months but cut its size.
The council's resolution, adopted by a 15-0 vote, would reduce the international police force from 300 to 250 and cut the military from 500 to 50 headquarters staff paid for by all U.N. members.
But Canada and Pakistan will again supplement the military force, this time with 650 Canadian soldiers and 350 Pakistanis, financed by Ottawa and Washington.
The request for the extension was made by Haitian President Rene Preval, who noted ongoing security problems that scared away any investments in the impoverished nation.
The operation, according to U.S. Ambassador Bill Richardson, would "further bolster the rule of law, development, democratization and peace in Haiti."
China and Russia this time supported the extension to Nov. 30 without problems, although both, for different reasons, oppose the Haiti mission.
China mainly had protested Haiti's ties with Taiwan, which it considers a renegade province.

Beijing had twice threatened to veto the U.N. military component of the operation in Haiti unless its numbers were reduced, prompting Canada to rescue the mission by paying for its soldiers and later sharing the burden for its troops and those of Pakistan with the United States.

One of the operation's main tasks was to train and monitor Haiti's fledgling police, which replaced the previous paramilitary contingents loyal to the military junta that overthrew elected President Jean-Bertrand Aristide in 1991.
The police have been cited for human rights abuses, having killed more than 45 people in the past year.

Aristide was restored to power three years later by a U.S.-led 22,000-member multinational force. The United Nations took over peacekeeping in March 1995 with 6,000 troops, a number that has been steadily reduced since then.

But in recent weeks Haitian demonstrators, some of them supporters of Aristide, burned tires and threw rocks at the U.N. peacekeepers, protesting the presence of foreign troops. Two days ago they called a general strike that shut down much of Haiti's second-largest city, Cap Haitian and parts of the capital of Port-au-Prince.

A growing number of Haitians are frustrated that the peacekeepers have been ordered not to intervene in Haitian disputes or violence. Others fear U.N. troops would be used to force acceptance of a plan to modernise Haiti's economy, thereby increasing unemployment in state-owned utilities.

Richardson noted concerns about the internal dynamics of politics in Haiti from Representative Benjamin Gilman, a New York Republican who is chairman of the U.S. House of Representatives) International Relations Committee. But he said Gilman supported the extension of the mandate.
Since the previous renewal was billed as the final extension, the Council changed the name of the mission for the third time. The latest name is the U.N. Transition Mission in Haiti or UNTMIH.
